a: given a drink of one Spirit
t: 'A drink of one Spirit' or 'a drink into one Spirit'?
p: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus add one small word, 'into.'

readings.w: The critical editions: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.en: given a drink of one Spirit
readings.plain: given a drink of one Spirit

readings.w: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (the King James Version, 'made to drink into one Spirit')
readings.en: given a drink into one Spirit
readings.plain: given a drink into one Spirit

why: The editions follow the shorter text, and the added 'into' may be an echo of 'into one body' earlier in the verse. The sense changes only a little.
b: The addition does not change the argument: the Spirit is the one drink all share.

p: A different Greek word lies behind the King James 'best gifts.'

readings.w: The critical editions: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.plain: greater gifts

readings.w: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the King James Version 'best gifts')
readings.plain: better gifts

why: All the critical editions print 'greater,' and it picks up the word used of prophecy and love in the neighboring verses (13:13; 14:5). 'Better' looks like a smoothing: 'greater' might suggest a rank among gifts, and scribes may have wanted to say they are more useful. The sense changes only a little.
b: In both readings Paul tells the Corinthians to be eager for gifts that count most for others; chapter 14 explains that prophecy is 'greater' than tongues because it builds up the church.

t: 'So that I can boast' or 'so that I may be burned'?
p: One letter's difference in the Greek gives 'boast' or 'be burned,' and the 'burned' reading has two forms.

readings.w: P46, Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), 048, minuscule 33 and the original hand of minuscule 1739, as listed in the NET Bible's textual note. NA28 and Westcott-Hort print this reading
readings.plain: so that I can boast

readings.w: Codex Ephraemi (C), Claromontanus (D), Augiensis (F), Boernerianus (G), L, minuscules 81, 1175 and the original hand of 1881, and the Latin witnesses (the Vulgate, ut ardeam), as listed in the NET Bible's textual note. The SBLGNT and Tyndale House print this future indicative form
readings.plain: so that I will be burned

readings.w: The Byzantine text (the NET note names Psi and the later hands of 1739 and 1881 with it) and the Textus Receptus (the King James Version, 'to be burned'); Tregelles also prints it. The ending looks like a subjunctive, but the verb is a future in form, and the NET Bible note calls the form impossible in Koine Greek
readings.plain: so that I may be burned

why: The 'boast' reading has the earliest Greek support, and it explains the other two: the Greek letters chi (χ) and theta (θ) are easy to swap, and a copyist who thought of martyrdom by fire could have made the change, which is how Metzger argues 'burned' arose, as Bill Mounce's summary of Metzger states. The two 'burned' forms differ from each other, which fits a later fix of an older text. This is a place where the Plain English Translation departs from the SBLGNT base text, which prints the 'burned' form with the omicron.
b: 'Boast' fits the context of 13:1-3 in which spiritual deeds are used for self-display: giving away one's goods, or even one's body, for the sake of one's own glory. 'Burned' reads as martyrdom by fire (compare Daniel 3), but Christian martyrdom by burning is not attested until after Paul wrote (Nero's persecution of AD 64), and the verse's third example is already the extreme one. A third idea is that the body is handed over into slavery to raise money for the poor; 1 Clement 55 reports that some Christians did this.

p: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus have a compound verb behind the King James 'never faileth.'

readings.w: The critical editions: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.plain: Love never collapses

readings.w: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (the King James Version, 'never faileth')
readings.plain: Love never falls away

why: All the critical editions print the simple verb. The compound, 'falls off,' may be a copyist's reach for a more familiar word. The sense is nearly the same.

a: I speak in tongues, and I thank God for it
t: 'I thank God' or 'I thank my God'?
p: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus add 'my' and change one verb ending.

readings.w: The critical editions: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ, πάντων ὑμῶν μᾶλλον γλώσσαις λαλῶ
readings.en: I thank God, I speak in tongues more than all of you
readings.plain: I speak in tongues, and I thank God for it

readings.w: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (the King James Version, 'I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all')
readings.orig: εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ μου, πάντων ὑμῶν μᾶλλον γλώσσαις λαλῶν
readings.en: I thank my God, speaking in tongues more than all of you
readings.plain: I speak in tongues, and I thank my God for it

why: The editions print the shorter text with the finite verb. The Byzantine form turns the speaking into a participle and adds 'my.' The meaning is the same.

p: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus change 'others' from a noun to an adjective.

readings.w: The critical editions: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.plain: the lips of others

readings.w: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (the King James Version, 'other lips')
readings.plain: other lips

why: The editions print 'the lips of others.' The Byzantine form may be a smoothing to match the 'other tongues' just before it. The difference is slight in English. The King James phrase 'men of other tongues' comes from the earlier word (heteroglossois), which is the same in both readings.

a: In the churches, the women are to be silent. They are not given permission to speak. Instead, let them submit, as the law also says.
t: Verses 34-35: here, or after verse 40? (goes with the next verse)
p: The Western tradition places verses 34-35 after verse 40; some scholars think they were added later.

readings.w: The great majority of Greek manuscripts; all printed Greek editions
readings.orig: αἱ γυναῖκες ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις σιγάτωσαν...
readings.en: the women should be silent in the churches
readings.plain: In the churches, the women are to be silent. They are not given permission to speak. Instead, let them submit, as the law also says.

readings.w: The verses after 14:40: Claromontanus (D, 06), Augiensis (F, 010), Boernerianus (G, 012) and minuscule 88, according to the Wikipedia articles on those manuscripts and its list of variants in 1 Corinthians. The Wikipedia article on Codex Boernerianus also says some Latin Vulgate manuscripts share the order. In Codex Fuldensis (the Vulgate, copied between 541 and 546) the scribe wrote verses 34-35 in the margin and gave verses 36-40 before them

why: Every Greek manuscript has 14:34-35, but a group of Western witnesses has them after 14:40, which is where the second reading puts them. The editions (NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House) keep them here, because the Greek manuscripts have them, in one place or the other. Gordon Fee and Philip Payne argue that the displacement shows the verses were first a marginal note. See the note on the verse and the deep dive in the chapter notes.
b: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (the King James Version) have small differences within the verse: 'your women' (hymon), 'it has been allowed' (epitetraptai) and the infinitive 'to submit' (hypotassesthai) in place of the command 'let them submit.' They do not change the sense. A fuller treatment: Fee, The First Epistle to the Corinthians; Payne, Man and Woman, One in Christ; Niccum's article on the manuscript evidence.

a: If they want to learn anything, their own husbands are the ones to question at home, since it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.
t: Verses 34-35: here, or after verse 40? (goes with the previous verse)
p: This goes with the variant on 14:34: the Western tradition places both verses after verse 40.

readings.w: The great majority of Greek manuscripts; all printed Greek editions
readings.en: if they want to learn anything
readings.plain: If they want to learn anything, their own husbands are the ones to question at home, since it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.

readings.w: The Western witnesses named on 14:34 (the verse follows 14:40)

why: This verse goes with 14:34, and the evidence is the same: the Western witnesses move both verses together after 14:40, while every Greek manuscript has them here. See the variant on 14:34 for the witnesses and the arguments.
b: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus read gynaixin, 'in women' (the plural), where the critical text has the singular gynaiki, 'for a woman'. This does not change the English.

a: what I am writing to you is the Lord's command
t: 'The Lord's command,' 'the Lord's,' or 'the Lord's commands'?
p: Manuscripts differ on whether 'command' is there, and whether it is singular or plural.

readings.w: The singular 'command' is printed by NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.en: that it is the Lord's command
readings.plain: what I am writing to you is the Lord's command

readings.w: The SBLGNT omits 'command' (the shorter text)
readings.plain: what I am writing to you is the Lord's

readings.w: The Byzantine text reads the plural; the Textus Receptus (the King James Version, 'the commandments of the Lord') adds the article before 'Lord'
readings.en: that they are the Lord's commands
readings.plain: what I am writing to you are the Lord's commands

why: Most critical editions print the singular 'command,' and the Plain English Translation follows them. The plural of the Byzantine text may come from a wish to make a general statement of everything Paul has written. The shorter text printed by the SBLGNT would mean the same thing, because 'the Lord's' would then carry the sense of 'the Lord's word.' This entry gives the editions only and names no manuscripts. The English is not much different in any reading.

a: If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.
t: 'He is not recognized' or 'let him be ignorant'?
p: One letter changes a statement ('he is not recognized') into a command ('let him be ignorant').

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House and Westcott-Hort print this reading
readings.en: he is not recognized (he is ignored)
readings.plain: If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.

readings.w: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (the King James Version, 'let him be ignorant'); Tregelles also prints it
readings.plain: If anyone does not recognize this, let him stay ignorant.

why: Most critical editions print the first reading. It is a wordplay with 'recognize' in 14:37: if anyone does not recognize Paul's authority, he is not recognized, meaning that God (or the church) will not recognize him, as in 8:3. The second is a command, and it makes Paul wash his hands of the matter. The Plain English Translation follows the editions that print the first. This entry names no manuscripts.
